statement: Colour adjectives follow the normal pattern (base form, -t, -e), except borrowed colours like lilla, orange, beige, pink and rosa, which never change.
explanation: Use the base form with an en-word (en rød bil, bilen er rød), add -t with an et-word (et rødt hus, huset er rødt), and add -e after den/det/de, possessives and in the plural (det røde hus, røde huse). Sort already ends in -t, so it stays sort with et-words, and grøn doubles the n before -e (grønne). Blå and grå take -t with et-words (et blåt øje) but normally no -e (de blå huse). Lilla, orange, beige, pink and rosa never change at all – a typical trap is writing "lillat" or "orangt".

examples.wrong: Hun bor i et hvid hus.
examples.right: Hun bor i et hvidt hus.
examples.note: Hus is an et-word, so the colour takes -t.

examples.wrong: Jeg har købt et lillat tæppe.
examples.right: Jeg har købt et lilla tæppe.
De grønne æbler er sure, men himlen er blå, og havet er blåt.
examples.note: Definite/plural -e (grøn doubles n); blå takes -t with an et-word.

statement: God follows the regular pattern (god/godt/gode), and godt is also the adverb meaning "well".
explanation: Use god with en-words (en god idé, maden er god), godt with et-words (et godt råd, vejret er godt) and gode after den/det/de, possessives and in the plural (de gode år, gode venner). Godt is also the adverb that tells how something is done: hun synger godt, jeg har det godt, jeg kan godt lide kaffe. The classic trap is god after a verb ("han synger god") – if the word describes the action, use godt.

examples.note: It describes how she dances, so use the adverb godt.

examples.right: Vi har et godt forhold til naboerne.
Mine gode venner kommer på lørdag.

statement: An adjective agrees with its noun both before it and after verbs like være and blive: base form for en-words, -t for et-words, -e in the plural and in the definite form.
explanation: First find the noun the adjective describes, even when it comes after er or bliver (huset er stort, bilerne er dyre). Indefinite singular: en stor have, et stort hus; plural always -e: store huse, husene er store. After den/det/de, denne/dette/disse, det her, possessives (mit) and genitives (Peters) the adjective always takes -e. The typical trap is writing -t after det or mit just because the noun is an et-word: mit store værelse, not "mit stort værelse". Also note that det + er + adjective + at takes -t: det er dyrt at bo her.

examples.wrong: Mit stort værelse vender mod syd.
examples.right: Mit store værelse vender mod syd.
examples.note: After a possessive: -e, even with an et-word.
Huset is an et-word, so the adjective after er takes -t.

examples.right: Disse varme dage er perfekte til stranden.
examples.note: After disse and in a plural predicative: -e.

statement: Some adjectives bend the pattern: no extra -t after -sk, -t or -e; ny and fri get -t and -e; lille becomes små in the plural; gammel, sikker and åben lose an e; short adjectives double the final consonant.
explanation: Adjectives ending in -sk (dansk, praktisk) and in -t (let, kort, træt) get no extra -t: et dansk pas, et let spørgsmål – but adjectives ending in -ig DO take -t: et vigtigt møde. Ny and fri take -t and -e (nyt, nye; frit, frie). Lille has the plural små (små børn), and adjectives ending in -e such as moderne and stille never change. Gammel, sikker, åben and enkel lose their last e before the -e ending (gamle, sikre, åbne, enkle), and short words with a short vowel double the consonant (grim → grimme, let → lette, smuk → smukke). Fremmed keeps its form in the neuter: et fremmed sprog.

examples.wrong: Vi bor i et gammelt hus med gammele vinduer.
examples.right: Vi bor i et gammelt hus med gamle vinduer.
examples.note: Gammel loses its e before the -e ending: gamle.

examples.right: De små børn leger i den lille have.
examples.note: Lille becomes små in the plural.

statement: Use al/alt with uncountable nouns (al maden, alt vandet) and hel/helt/hele with countable nouns (en hel dag, hele huset); helt is also an adverb meaning "completely".
explanation: Al (en-words) and alt (et-words) mean "all of" something you cannot count: al maden, al sneen, alt vandet, alt arbejdet. For the whole of something countable use hel: en hel dag, et helt år, and hele before a definite noun or a possessive: hele dagen, hele mit liv. On its own, alt means "everything" (hun har glemt alt). Helt before an adjective means "completely": helt ny, helt færdig. The classic trap is "al dagen" – a day can be counted, so it must be hele dagen.

examples.note: Mælk is an uncountable en-word: al.

examples.right: Vi boede der et helt år, og lejligheden var helt ny.
examples.note: Et helt år = a whole year; helt ny = completely new.

da: Al, alt, alle eller hel, helt, hele
en: Al, alt, alle or hel, helt, hele – all forms
statement: Choose by countability and number: al/alt with uncountables, alle with countable plurals (and alone = everybody), hel/helt/hele for one whole thing – and hele before a plural means "whole, not cut up".
explanation: Ask two questions: can the noun be counted, and is it singular or plural? Uncountable: al maden, alt tøjet. Countable plural: alle børnene, alle mine venner; on its own alle means "everybody" and alt means "everything". Countable singular: en hel pizza, et helt år, hele dagen, hele klassen. Hele before a plural does not mean "all" but "whole": to hele kyllinger (whole chickens). The common trap is "hele eleverne" – for all the pupils say alle eleverne, or hele klassen.

examples.note: Klassen is one countable group: hele.

examples.right: Alle var glade, og alt gik godt.
